result: The authors used two-photon calcium imaging to record responses from thousands of V1 superficial-layer neurons simultaneously in three awake macaques, identifying 10,168 neurons with 92.3% tuned to orientation or spatial frequency. Recordings were performed at two cortical depths in the first two monkeys and at a single depth in the third monkey after similar results were observed at both depths.
evaluation: All reviewers praised the methodology and large dataset. Reviewer 1 stated 'the approach was well-executed' and highlighted the 'considerably high spatial resolution' allowing sampling of 'thousands of verified superficial-layer V1 neurons.' Reviewer 2 noted 'A major strength of this work is that the model-fitting was done on a large population of simultaneously recorded neurons' and called it 'an important data set.' The editor confirmed 'the large data set and strength of the method used that allowed for spatial analysis of neuronal responses in macaque V1.'

result: V1 superficial-layer neurons exhibited various degrees of eye preferences consistent with classical findings, with ocular dominance index (ODI) ranging from -1 (complete contralateral preference) to +1 (complete ipsilateral preference). The frequency distributions of ODIs suggest more binocular neurons than monocular neurons in V1 superficial layers, and ocular dominance maps were similar at two cortical depths suggesting the presence of ocular dominance columns.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as consistent with established knowledge. Reviewer 1 noted the work 'corroborating what has been shown previously using electrophysiological techniques with now much finer spatial resolution' and that the imaging technique 'allowed the authors to evaluate the monocular and binocular response profiles of V1 neurons that are situated within neighboring ocular dominance columns, a novel feat.' No reviewer challenged these characterizations of ocular dominance.

result: During monocular stimulation, neurons preferring the stimulated eye exhibited significantly stronger responses compared to those preferring both eyes. Neurons with more negative ODIs responded stronger to contralateral eye stimulation, those with more positive ODIs responded stronger to ipsilateral eye stimulation, and responses declined as neurons became more binocular. More monocular neurons (ODIs farther from 0) exhibited stronger responses compared to more binocular neurons (ODIs closer to 0) when considering responses to the preferred eye.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these monocular response findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 stated 'As expected, the contra-eye dominated neurons responded strongly with a contra-eye only stimulus. The ipsi-eye dominated neurons responded strongly with an ipsi-eye only stimulus.' The editor noted 'consistency of responses across animals' as supporting the evidence. These findings align with expected patterns of ocular dominance.

result: During binocular stimulation, responses of neurons preferring either eye were suppressed on average while those preferring both eyes were enhanced, resulting in similar neuronal responses irrespective of eye preferences and an overall response level similar to monocular viewing. Linear regression verified significant dependence of binocular modulation on absolute ODI (y=-0.36x+0.14, p<0.001), with binocular neurons more enhanced and monocular neurons more suppressed by binocular stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed this key finding. Reviewer 1 stated 'They found a strong relationship in their data: neurons that exhibited a greater preference for one eye or the other (high ocular dominance) were more likely to be suppressed under binocular stimulation, whereas neurons that are more equivalently driven by each other (low ocular dominance) were more likely to be enhanced.' Reviewer 2 noted 'The surprise was responses to a binocular stimulus. The responses were similarly weak across the entire population, regardless of each neuron's ocular dominance.' The editor confirmed 'The conclusions of this paper are well supported by the data.'

result: A neuronally realistic model incorporating ocular dominance-dependent divisive interocular inhibition and binocular summation was proposed to account for the findings. The model showed adequate goodness of fit (0.87-0.94 for monocular conditions, 0.88-0.92 for binocular), with monocular response functions exhibiting drastic changes as a function of ODI while binocular response functions remained largely flat. Modeling indicated that interocular divisive suppression (more prominent with monocular neurons) and binocular summation (more prominent with binocular neurons) together produce the nearly flat binocular response function.
evaluation: Reviewers praised the modeling work. Reviewer 1 stated 'The binocular responses were well-fitted by a model that institutes divisive normalization between the eyes that accounts for both the suppression and enhancement phenomena' and noted the authors 'reify the importance of incorporating ocular dominance in computational models of binocular combination.' Reviewer 2 emphasized 'the model-fitting was done on a large population of simultaneously recorded neurons' as 'an advancement over previous work' and stated 'Their data support their conclusion.' The editor confirmed 'fitness of modeling' as part of the compelling evidence.

result: The findings imply that significant ocular dominance may stem from a release of interocular suppression during monocular stimulation rather than a lack of binocular combination. The median binocular neuronal responses were only marginally higher than monocular responses from each eye, with the overall similarity between monocular and binocular responses likely playing a significant role in maintaining stable vision in both viewing conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted these interpretations. Reviewer 2 stated 'The implication of their finding is that strong ocular dominance is the result of release from interocular suppression by a monocular stimulus, rather than the lack of binocular combination as many traditional studies have assumed. This could significantly advance our understanding of the binocular combination circuitry of V1.' Reviewer 1 noted 'The conclusions of this paper are well supported by the data' and that authors 'deftly contextualize these important findings in the literature.'

result: The current study's results reveal that monocular neurons show much stronger responses to stimulation in the preferred eye compared to binocular neurons under the same monocular stimulation, and indicate enhanced responses in binocular neurons to binocular stimulation. These findings differ from Dougherty et al., 2019, which found similar responses to monocular stimulation between monocular and binocular neurons.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these differences from prior work. Reviewer 1 stated 'The authors deftly contextualize these important findings in the literature while also acknowledging the limitations of the methodology employed.' The editor noted 'The authors have addressed the major comments from reviewers and improved the manuscript through relation to prior literature.' The discrepancies with Dougherty et al. are acknowledged and discussed by the authors.

result: Two-photon imaging can only sample neurons from superficial layers, while binocular neurons also exist in deeper layers and neurons in the input layer are affected by feedback from downstream binocular neurons. Calcium signals are relatively slow and cannot capture the fast dynamics of neuronal responses.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged these limitations. Reviewer 3 stated 'Given that these recordings are made optically, these results reflect primarily activations of neurons in the superficial layers of the cortex...This means that the sample of neurons forming this data set is not fully representative of the population of binocular neurons within the visual cortex.' Reviewer 1 noted 'The authors address the limitations of the methodology and have calibrated the interpretations accordingly.' The editor confirmed authors 'addressing specific limitations of the method used.'

result: Calcium signals indicated by GCaMP5 display a linear relationship to neuronal spike rates within 10-150 Hz, but weaker and stronger signals outside this range are more nonlinear and may appear different than electrode-recorded effects. The differences in population responses between monocular and binocular stimulations revealed by this study might be less pronounced when measured with electrode recording.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised this concern but then dismissed it: 'The nonlinear interocular suppression found in this study, could potentially be partially exaggerated by the nonlinear properties of calcium signals. One of the authors of this study has previously reported that the particular GCaMP used in this study has a nice proportional relationship with firing rate of a neuron. So the concern of exaggeration probably does not apply to this particular study.' This represents acknowledged uncertainty about potential methodological effects, though reviewers ultimately accepted the findings.

result: It remains unclear whether discrepancies with prior electrode recording studies are caused by differences in temporal resolutions between techniques. Electrode recordings capture responses over 50-200ms while calcium signals capture aggregated responses over up to 1000ms, which should theoretically reduce rather than exaggerate differences, though neuronal response changes beyond 200ms may contribute to discrepancies.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this uncertainty without resolving it. Reviewer 1 stated 'Future work would do well to combine the spatial power of 2P imaging with the temporal power of electrophysiology to assess ocular dominance-dependent binocular combination across the V1 laminar microcircuit.' This suggests the temporal resolution issue remains an open question requiring future investigation.
